text: A poet, a playwright, an aristocrat and an army officer, all the same man, once tried to build a country out of the rubble the First World War left behind. Igor Bezinović approaches him through dramatic reconstruction and documentary aside, so the film keeps stepping out of the past in order to look at it. Documentary, comedy and history are the three labels it carries, and they do not sit quietly together. Fascism at its beginning, played at the scale of costume, slogan and personal vanity, becomes legible in a way solemnity tends to hide, and 112 minutes is long enough to watch a mood harden into a program. Made in Croatia, in Croatian, about an Italian who arrived certain that history was his to author. It took a Tiger Award.

Rusty James wants the gang war back, and the gang war is over. What he actually has is his brother's reputation, which he did not earn and cannot escape, and a neighborhood that treats the old violence as a story rather than a threat. He is described as absent-minded, and the word holds: his attention is fixed on a better year that has already closed. Coppola built it as a crime picture largely uninterested in crime — 94 minutes, one small territory, the same few streets crossed again and again. Romance is in the picture too, real and small, one more thing Rusty James lacks the attention to notice. It carries a place on the Golden Shell list. What stays is the ache under the swagger: not wanting a fight so much as wanting to matter the way someone else already does.

A road through France, driven at several distances from the wedding day, carries the whole chronology of a marriage. Mark and Joanna Wallace are on their way to see a client with money; the trip keeps opening into earlier trips, so courtship, comfort, irritation and betrayal occupy adjacent minutes instead of a sequence. The client is the excuse; the itinerary is the subject. The screenplay took the Academy Award for original writing, and that shuffling is its entire method — a marriage is remembered this way even though it cannot be lived this way. Stanley Donen runs 112 minutes of a British production across French roads and keeps the surface pleasant while the couple keep overhearing their younger selves. Infidelity here is mutual, which holds the ledger even and leaves the sympathy uncomfortably divided. The accounting underneath is less friendly.

In 1937 the Japanese army took Nanjing, then the capital of the Republic of China, and what followed took six weeks to do and much longer to say. Lu Chuan made the film in China, in Chinese, at 132 minutes, which means it answers to an audience for whom this is not distant history. The difficulty of such a subject is arithmetic: tens of thousands of soldiers and civilians killed is a figure, and a figure cannot be photographed, so the work has to keep locating single rooms, single decisions, single faces inside the total. That is a formal problem before it is a moral one, and here the two are not separable. Its Chinese title repeats the name of the city, as if once would not register. What stands to be lost in a film like this is not suspense but proportion.

Non Educated Delinquents is what the letters stand for, and the boy the film follows began by winning school prizes. John McGill is bright, and being bright turns out to be no protection when everyone around him has already set the expectation low. Peter Mullan tracks the conversion in stages — victim to avenger, scholar to delinquent, altar boy to glue sniffer — and then attempts the harder move, which is the way back. That is where the 124 minutes earn their length, since a reputation is far easier to acquire than to return. An English-language drama produced out of France, it puts its weight on how quickly a description becomes a life. What is at risk is not his survival. It is whether he can be believed harmless again.

The lights go out in an office building, and when they come back a man is dead on the pavement and an accountant upstairs has lost two years. David Stillwell cannot say where the time went, or why the dead man means nothing to him. Edward Dmytryk turns that into a detective story whose evidence is stored in the wrong place: not in files or witnesses but inside the investigator, who has every reason to distrust what he finds. A rookie private eye and a reluctant old flame are the only help on offer, and neither is well equipped for it. At 109 minutes it stays lean, detail by detail, and the stakes are strange for a thriller — solving the case means agreeing to be whoever the answer says he is. It holds a Golden Shell.

A housewife learns she is pregnant and, instead of settling into the news, leaves town. The freedom she is looking for is not the romantic kind; the film sends her out to reconsider decisions she made when nobody asked her to think about them. Francis Ford Coppola shot it in 1969 at 101 minutes, an American picture with almost nothing in it but road and reconsideration. Its smallness is the design: one woman, a head start, and no destination she is willing to name. The year gives the premise its charge, a wife driving away from the house she is expected to be inside. It sits on the Golden Shell list. What stands to be lost is not a marriage. It is the possibility that a person who has never been alone will find she does not much like her own company.

A country estate in disrepair, one summer day, a party of friends and acquaintances who know each other slightly too well. The house is described as dilapidated, which is the only judgment the premise makes out loud. Nikita Mikhalkov keeps all 98 minutes inside that property, and the decision has consequences: nobody can leave a scene without walking into the next one, and the talk has to carry everything a plot would otherwise handle. The people are comfortable enough to be bored and articulate enough to make the boredom sound like philosophy, which is a particular kind of cruelty to arrange. It was made in the Soviet Union in 1977 and looks back at bourgeois leisure of the late nineteenth century, a vantage that changes how the complaints land. Nobody in the house is working. Everybody in the house is exhausted.

Buzykin cannot say a true sentence to either woman, and it is not cruelty that stops him. He translates English literature, teaches at an institute, and manages his wife and his lover with the same anxious courtesy, which is why both of them are unhappy and neither is deceived. Georgiy Daneliya keeps it to 89 minutes and lets the days repeat: the same evasions, the same apologies, the same promises broken because he cannot bear to disappoint whoever is standing in front of him. It is filed as a comedy, and it is one, in the way a joke about one's own life is funny. It went out as an international submission to the Academy Awards, and it took the Vasilyev Brothers State Prize of the RSFSR.

Seven months of paperwork stand between an old musician and one concert. Mamo is Kurdish, lives in Iran, and wants to play in Iraqi Kurdistan; the band is his own ten sons, the bus is already falling apart, and the border is the least negotiable thing in the film. Bahman Ghobadi builds the journey out of its obstructions, and the one that matters most arrives when the party stops for Hesho, a singer forbidden to perform in public in Iran and more forbidden still in the company of men. What is at stake is not the concert but whether a performance can be carried across a border that does not want it. An Austrian production, spoken in Kurdish, 108 minutes long. Mamo also carries a vision he refuses to discuss, and it travels with him.

A motor-home makes a good office for two people who take small amounts and move on before anyone adds them up. Betty and Victor are mismatched in nearly every way and exactly matched in trade, touring France without being noticed, treating fraud as a routine rather than an adventure. The pleasure of the setup is its scale: swindling practised like housekeeping, with the same attention to schedules and small change. Then a piece of international money business arrives, far larger than anything their method was built for, and takes them out of the country and out of their depth. Claude Chabrol spends the 105 minutes on the partnership itself, whose rules are never stated aloud and are entirely understood by both. What they stand to lose is not the money. It is the small life that worked because it was small.

A mother's memory starts to fail, and the family it had been holding together has to sit in one room again. Yeşim Ustaoğlu puts the crisis in Istanbul, where the practical question — who takes her, and for how long — cannot be raised without reopening everything the adults had agreed not to say. Illness in films is often a device for producing grief on schedule; here the movement is administrative, a matter of arrangements and obligations, and the arrangements turn out to be where the family history was stored. 112 minutes, in Turkish, with French production behind it. The premise leaves nobody free to be simply dutiful or simply selfish, which is the harder arrangement and the more common one.

Charles Serking lectures on poetry and drinks with a commitment he gives to nothing else. He surfaces from one haze long enough to catch a bus back to Los Angeles, where the appetites resume on arrival and the day is organized by whatever is nearest. Marco Ferreri directs, and the David di Donatello for Best Director went to him for it, which is an odd prize for a film so plainly uninterested in being liked. The production is Italian and the degradation is American; the distance between the two keeps the picture from either scolding its poet or admiring him. 101 minutes spent with a man who has stopped negotiating with anyone, including himself. Whether that is a life or a performance is what the premise keeps open.
